documents.title: The Overnight Overdraft
documents.subtitle: Concurrent Withdrawals and Lost Updates
documents.body:
Your team is on-call for a challenger bank's payment platform. At 02:14, PagerDuty fires: account balance monitoring reports 23 accounts with negative balances. No overdraft facility has been granted. You pull up the logs.

The system processes 2,500 withdrawal requests per second across 4 application pods. The account balance is stored in a `balance` column in PostgreSQL. The withdrawal flow is: (1) read balance, (2) check balance >= amount, (3) if yes, update balance, (4) post journal entry.

Post-mortem reveals: at peak load, 3% of accounts were overdrawn. No exceptions were logged. All transactions completed successfully from the application's perspective. What is the root cause of the overnight overdrafts, and what is the most appropriate primary fix? Connection pool exhaustion: under load, threads wait for connections and then act on balances they read before the wait. Fix by enlarging the HikariCP pool and adding a connection validation query. Lost update between read and write. Fix by locking the account row first — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE — so concurrent withdrawals on one account run one after another before the balance check. Lost update between read and write. Make check and debit one statement: UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - :amt WHERE id = :id AND balance >= :amt; 0 rows updated = insufficient funds. A missing index on accounts forces full table scans. Under load PostgreSQL escalates row locks to table locks, so transactions interfere with each other. Fix by adding a covering index on (id, balance). You deploy the atomic conditional UPDATE fix. Three days later, a different type of overdraft is reported: a customer's available balance showed £600, they withdrew £500, but the account was then overdrawn when a pending card authorisation of £200 settled. Under which scenario does the atomic UPDATE still produce incorrect results? When the UPDATE checks the ledger balance (£600) but the real limit is the available balance (£400 after a £200 card hold).…

documents.title: The Double Charge
documents.subtitle: Idempotency and Duplicate Payment Detection
documents.body:
Customer service has escalated 50 double-charge complaints in the past week. Investigation shows: mobile app clients use an aggressive retry policy — if no response within 3 seconds, they retry up to 3 times. Under load, the payment service occasionally takes 4–6 seconds to respond.

The current idempotency implementation checks for an existing payment by idempotency key before inserting. The idempotency key is a UUID generated by the client before the first attempt. The current code uses: (1) SELECT payment WHERE idempotency_key = ?, (2) if found, return existing result, (3) if not found, INSERT new payment and process. What is the fundamental flaw in this approach? The key is generated by the client. Client keys cannot be trusted: two different phones can produce the same UUID, so the server should generate the key and return it on the first response. The SELECT reads without a lock. Changing it to SELECT ... FOR UPDATE would make the second request wait until the first one has inserted its row, closing the gap. Check-then-insert is not atomic. Two retries can both run the SELECT, both find nothing, and both INSERT before either commits — so both payments are processed. The 24-hour key expiry is too short. Customers who retry the next day get charged again, so keys should be kept permanently to make duplicate detection complete. You replace check-then-insert with a UNIQUE constraint on idempotency_key. A retry arrives after the original payment has completed, and its INSERT fails with DataIntegrityViolationException. What should the service return? HTTP 409 Conflict. The request conflicts with a resource that already exists, and the client should treat 409 as "already done" and fetch the payment separately. HTTP 200 (or the original 201) with the original payment in the body — look up the payment by its key and return exactly the response the first request received. HTTP 500 Internal Server Error. A constraint violation is an unexpected database error; returning…

documents.title: The Lost Event
documents.subtitle: Database and Kafka Dual-Write Problem
documents.body:
A payment service saves a payment record to PostgreSQL and then publishes a PaymentProcessedEvent to Kafka. Downstream services (notification, analytics, AML) consume the Kafka event to trigger their workflows.

In production, 1-in-10,000 payments results in a complaint: the customer's payment was processed (money moved), but they received no confirmation notification, and the AML system has no record of the transaction. Investigation reveals: the service crashed after the PostgreSQL commit but before the Kafka publish. What is the name of this consistency problem and what is the correct architectural fix? It is normal eventual consistency. Model the flow as a Saga, and when the Kafka publish fails, run a compensating transaction that reverses the payment so both sides agree again. It is an at-most-once delivery problem. Enable producer idempotence (enable.idempotence=true) and retry the send indefinitely until Kafka acknowledges it. It is the dual-write problem. Write the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the payment; a separate relay then publishes outbox rows to Kafka. It is a Kafka availability problem. Put a circuit breaker around the producer; while Kafka is down, buffer events in Redis and flush them once Kafka recovers. You implement the Outbox Pattern. The outbox poller reads pending events from the `outbox_events` table, publishes to Kafka, and marks the event as `published=true`. What failure mode does this architecture still have? The relay can publish the same event twice: if it crashes after Kafka acknowledges the send but before it marks the row as published, it sends that row again after restart. Events can arrive out of order: the relay reads rows in batches, and a batch can be published in a different order from the order the payments were committed. The outbox table becomes a write bottleneck: every payment now performs two inserts in the same transaction, which roughly halves the write throughput of the payment table.…

documents.title: The Hot Account
documents.subtitle: Concurrent Balance Updates at Scale
documents.body:
A UK challenger bank handles HMRC (tax authority) payroll credit runs: 3 million employees' salaries paid via BACS within a 2-hour window. This routes through a single HMRC suspense account at the bank that receives 3,000 credits and debits per second.

The current implementation uses SELECT FOR UPDATE on the account row for every transaction. Under this load, p99 latency for account updates has reached 8 seconds. The lock queue depth grows to 1,200 waiting transactions. Transactions are timing out at the application layer, causing retries that further amplify the problem. SELECT FOR UPDATE is creating an 8-second lock queue at 3,000 TPS. What architectural change provides the highest throughput while maintaining exact balance correctness? Raise PostgreSQL max_connections and the application pool size, so more requests can wait in the lock queue at the same time instead of being rejected. Replace SELECT FOR UPDATE with optimistic locking (@Version). There is no lock wait at all; the rare conflicting update is simply retried by the application. Send all writes for the hot account through one ordered queue with a single consumer, which applies them in sequence and can batch them in short windows (e.g. 100 ms). Split the balance into 10 sub-balances, spread debits and credits across them, and compute the account balance as the sum of the sub-balances when it is needed. You deploy queue-based serialisation with one consumer. During a Kubernetes rolling deployment, the queue consumer pod is briefly unavailable. The queue depth grows to 50,000 events in 90 seconds. What design prevents this single point of failure while maintaining serial balance updates? Run 3 consumer replicas in one consumer group so the HMRC events are shared across them and processed in parallel, which also removes the single point of failure. Key the topic by account ID so all HMRC events share one partition, and run several replicas. One owns that partition; if it dies, another takes over in…

documents.title: The Failed Saga
documents.subtitle: Partial Payment Failure and Compensation
documents.body:
A cross-border payment flow consists of three steps executed across three microservices: (1) FX Service — quote and lock an exchange rate, (2) Debit Service — debit the customer's GBP account, (3) Credit Service — credit the beneficiary's USD account.

In production, step 3 (Credit) fails 0.3% of the time due to the beneficiary bank's API returning 503 errors. Currently, the system logs the failure and alerts. The GBP debit has already been posted. The customer's money is debited but never arrives at the destination. Steps 1 and 2 have succeeded. Step 3 (Credit) fails with a 503 from the beneficiary bank. What is the correct architectural response to maintain financial consistency? Run the flow as a Saga: when step 3 fails, the orchestrator runs compensations in reverse order — refund the GBP debit, then release the FX rate lock. Use two-phase commit (XA) across the three services. If step 3 fails, the transaction coordinator rolls back steps 1 and 2 automatically, so no compensation logic is needed. Retry step 3 with exponential backoff until it succeeds. A 503 means the beneficiary bank is temporarily down, and retrying avoids the cost of undoing steps 1 and 2. Leave the payment in PARTIALLY_COMPLETE and put it on a manual-review queue, so operations staff decide case by case whether to retry the credit or refund the customer. The Saga triggers the compensating transaction (reverse the GBP debit). The Debit Service's compensation step itself fails: the service returns HTTP 500 (the service is restarting). The Saga orchestrator cannot complete the reversal. What must happen next? Mark the Saga FAILED and page the on-call engineer, who triggers the refund by hand once the Debit Service is back. Automatic retries risk refunding twice. Compensate only what you can: release the FX lock now, and accept that the GBP debit stays in place until someone notices that the Debit Service has recovered. Credit the customer from a different service instead of reversing the…

documents.title: The Cascading Timeout
documents.subtitle: Thread Pool Exhaustion and Cascading Failure
documents.body:
Your payment authorisation service calls three downstream services on every request: FraudCheck (200ms avg), BIC Validation (50ms avg), and Account Lookup (30ms). The service runs with a shared thread pool of 200 threads and processes 1,800 requests/second.

At 11:23, FraudCheck begins responding slowly — P99 climbs from 200ms to 8 seconds over 10 minutes. At 11:34, PagerDuty fires: payment authorisation service health check failing. All 200 threads are blocked waiting on FraudCheck responses. BIC Validation and Account Lookup — both healthy — are receiving zero traffic. The entire payment service is down because one downstream dependency degraded. What is the root cause of the complete service outage, and what architectural pattern was missing? Thread pool exhaustion: all 200 shared threads are stuck waiting on FraudCheck, so healthy dependencies cannot be reached. Missing pattern: a bulkhead — one bounded pool per dependency. Network saturation: FraudCheck's slow responses keep many connections open and use up the network capacity of the payment service, so BIC Validation and Account Lookup calls cannot get through. CPU starvation: FraudCheck responses are expensive to parse at this volume, so the payment service host runs out of CPU and every request — whatever its dependency — slows down together. The 30-second FraudCheck timeout is far too long. Cutting it to 500 ms would release threads quickly enough that the shared pool never fills up, so no other change is needed. You implement bulkhead isolation. FraudCheck is now allocated a dedicated pool of 60 threads with a 1-second timeout. During the next FraudCheck degradation, payment service stays up but 60% of payments are declined with FRAUD_CHECK_TIMEOUT errors. The business wants degraded-mode operation: skip FraudCheck and approve low-risk transactions when FraudCheck is unavailable. What is the correct implementation? documents.title: The Kafka Rebalance Storm
documents.subtitle: Consumer Group Rebalance Loop Halting AML Processing
documents.body:
Your AML transaction-monitoring service consumes the Kafka topic `transactions.completed` (24 partitions) with 3 consumer pods. Each pod runs one consumer thread and screens records one at a time: every record needs a sanctions-screening API call (about 650 ms) and a Redis lookup (about 15 ms). At normal volume (about 240 records per minute) the consumers keep up, so each poll() returns only a handful of records.

To get ahead of growth, the team scales to 11 pods. The new pods start one after another, each join causes a rebalance, and a backlog builds up while partitions move. Within minutes every consumer is stuck in a loop: it joins, polls, is removed from the group, and rejoins. Lag keeps rising and no AML alerts are produced. After 40 minutes the team rolls back to 3 pods, but the lag (about 9,600 records) does not drain. What is causing the continuous rebalance loop, and why did it never happen with 3 pods? Too many consumers for the partition count. Kafka needs at least two partitions per consumer; with 11 consumers on 24 partitions the group coordinator becomes unstable and keeps rebalancing. A full poll outlasts max.poll.interval.ms: 500 × ~0.665 s ≈ 330 s > 300 s, so the consumer is removed and the next full poll repeats it. With 3 pods there was no backlog. A coordinator limitation: when ten or more consumers join a group at about the same time, the group coordinator enters a failed state and keeps triggering rebalances until consumers are restarted one by one. The sanctions API rate limit: 11 pods calling it at the same time exceed its quota, the calls time out, and the timeouts alone make each poll exceed max.poll.interval.ms. You are back on 3 pods with about 9,600 records of lag. What is the right way to drain the lag safely, without duplicate AML alerts? Cut max.poll.records to 50 (~33 s per poll), scale out again (up to 24 consumers can be active), and make alert creation idempotent. Reset the group's offsets to the latest position so monitoring…

documents.title: The GC Storm
documents.subtitle: JVM Full GC Pauses Breaching Payment Authorisation SLO
documents.body:
Payment authorisation service SLO: P99 latency < 200ms. For the past two weeks, the SLO is breached every weekday between 08:00 and 09:00 (London market open). P99 spikes to 4–8 seconds for 2–3 minutes, then self-resolves.

GC logs (enabled with -Xlog:gc*) show Full GC events lasting 3–6 seconds during the spike window. Heap is configured at 8GB. The service runs Java 21 with G1GC (default). At 3× load G1 cannot meet the pause target, falls further and further behind, and finally falls back to a Full GC to catch up. Kubernetes CPU throttling: at market open the pods reach their CPU limit, the GC threads are descheduled in the middle of a collection, and pauses that normally take milliseconds stretch into seconds. Heap resizing: the heap grows from 2 GB (-Xms2g) towards 8 GB (-Xmx8g) as load rises, and each expansion forces G1 to rebuild its region layout with a stop-the-world Full GC. Objects ≥ 2 MB are humongous (half a 4 MB region) and need contiguous old-gen regions. At 3× load they fragment the heap, evacuation fails, and G1 falls back to Full GC. documents.title: The Phantom Trade
documents.subtitle: Database Isolation Failure in FX Exposure Limit Enforcement
documents.body:
An FX trading system enforces a £500,000 maximum exposure per trader per currency pair per day. The check runs as: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM fx_positions WHERE trader_id = ? AND currency_pair = ? documents.title: The Penny Drift
documents.subtitle: Floating-Point Money, Rounding and Fee Allocation
documents.body:
A multi-currency wallet converts balances between currencies and splits every merchant fee three ways: platform 50%, partner 30%, card network 20%. documents.title: The Database Migration Deadline
documents.subtitle: DDL Lock Queues on a Live 800M-Row Table
documents.body:
Compliance needs a new column on `payment_transactions` (PostgreSQL 16, 800 million rows, 20,000 inserts per second). The migration is:

ALTER TABLE payment_transactions ADD COLUMN risk_score NUMERIC(5,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00;

In staging it finished in 40 ms. In production, at 10:05, it caused a 4-minute total outage of the payment API: every insert and every read on the table hung, connection pools filled up, and health checks failed. When the DBA killed the migration session, everything recovered within seconds.

pg_stat_activity during the incident showed a reporting query that had been reading `payment_transactions` for 3 hours, the ALTER TABLE waiting behind it, and about 2,000 application queries waiting behind the ALTER TABLE. documents.title: The Reconciliation Break
documents.subtitle: Business-Day Cut-offs, Time Zones and Timing Breaks
documents.body:
Every night at 02:00 a reconciliation job matches the internal card ledger against the card scheme's settlement file for the previous business day. The scheme defines the business day in London local time. Reconciliation has been clean all summer.

documents.title: The Memory Leak
documents.subtitle: JVM OOM from Unbounded Cache Accumulating PDF Byte Arrays
documents.body:
Payment gateway pods restart every 4–6 hours with OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. This started exactly 3 weeks ago after releasing a new PDF statement generation feature. Normal pod memory usage: 400MB. Pods restart at ~3.8GB heap used.

documents.title: The Alert Fatigue
documents.subtitle: 420 PagerDuty Pages in One Week Hide a Real Outage
documents.body:
The payment processing team receives 420 PagerDuty pages in one week. 65% are P2 alerts for P99 latency > 500ms. P50 latency is healthy at 45ms. P99 is naturally spiky — GC pauses and 1–2% of slow downstream API calls push individual requests above 500ms even during normal operation.

documents.title: The Config Disaster
documents.subtitle: Copy-Paste Error in Deployment Pipeline Causes 12,000 False Declines

documents.title: The Slow Query Bomb
documents.subtitle: Billing Job Takes 4 Minutes in Staging, 6+ Hours in Production
documents.body:
The monthly billing job runs fine in staging: 50,000 customers, completes in 4 minutes. First production run with 8.2 million customers has been running for 6 hours without completing. The core query:

SELECT c.id, c.email, SUM(t.amount) as total_billed
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN transactions t ON c.id = t.customer_id
WHERE t.created_at >= '2026-10-01'

documents.title: The API Breaking Change
documents.subtitle: Silent Breaking Change in Payment API Breaks Three Client Integrations
documents.body:
The payments API v1 has been live for 18 months. It returns:
```json
{ "status": "SUCCESS", "amount": 100.00, "reference": "PAY-123" }
```
The team deploys a new version that improves the response:
```json
{ "status": "COMPLETED", "amount": "100.00", "currency": "GBP", "reference": "PAY-123" }
```
Changes: (1) `status` value renamed from `SUCCESS` to `COMPLETED`, (2) `amount` type changed from JSON number to JSON string, (3) `currency` field added.

Only the status rename is breaking. A number can always be read as a string, so the amount change is safe, and adding a field is always backward compatible. Only the amount type change is breaking. documents.title: The Audit Gap
documents.subtitle: 5-Year Regulatory Audit Request Reveals 3.5 Years of Missing Records
documents.body:
The FCA requests all actions on 47 high-risk customer accounts for a 5-year period. The compliance team runs the extraction. 23 of the 47 accounts have missing records: audit events exist for the last 18 months but nothing before.

documents.subtitle: Non-atomic read-modify-write corrupts transaction counters under concurrent load
documents.body: A fraud detection service tracks per-merchant transaction counts in real time. Each incoming payment request increments a counter for the merchant ID. The service runs as a singleton Spring bean inside a high-throughput API gateway handling 50,000 requests per second. Counters are read every 10 seconds to trigger fraud alerts when thresholds are crossed. Under concurrent load, the non-atomic get-then-put sequence allows two threads to read the same stale counter value, both compute an increment, and write back — causing one increment to be silently lost. At peak load, counters can undercount by 10-30%, causing the fraud detection system to miss velocity thresholds and fail to block fraudulent merchants in time. HashMap provides no thread-safety guarantees. Two threads executing recordTransaction() concurrently can both read the same value (e.g., 42) on line 11, both compute newValue = 43, and both write 43 back — resulting in a net increment of 1 instead of 2. At high concurrency, this lost-update race can occur thousands of times per second. Concurrent structural changes (resizing) can also corrupt the map itself — on older JDKs even causing infinite loops in get().

documents.title: Concurrent Withdrawal Race
documents.subtitle: Database MVCC & SELECT FOR UPDATE
documents.body: Two API requests arrive simultaneously to withdraw funds from the same account. Without a row-level lock, both reads return the same balance snapshot before either write commits, allowing both to proceed even when only one should. A customer with $1,000 withdraws $800 and $300 at the same moment. One of them should be rejected, but both succeed — $1,100 is paid out — and because the second write overwrites the first, the balance ends at $700. The $800 debit disappears from the balance with no error, and the books no longer match the cash that left the bank. PostgreSQL's MVCC lets plain SELECTs read the latest committed data without taking locks (under READ COMMITTED, each statement sees a fresh snapshot). Two concurrent transactions therefore both read the same balance, both pass the balance check, and both compute a new balance from that stale value. When they write, the second UPDATE simply overwrites the first — a classic lost update. Both withdrawals complete without error, but the final balance reflects only one of them.

documents.title: Idempotency Key Race Condition
documents.subtitle: Check-Then-Act & UNIQUE Constraint
documents.body: A payment client retries a failed request and sends the same idempotency key twice within milliseconds. The service checks whether the key already exists before inserting; two concurrent retries both see 'not found' and both proceed to insert a duplicate payment. A customer is charged twice for a single purchase. The merchant receives two settlement entries, support costs spike, and the institution faces regulatory exposure for double-billing without a compensating reversal. The check (existsByIdempotencyKey) and the act (save) are two separate database operations with no lock or atomic guarantee between them. Under READ COMMITTED isolation, both concurrent transactions execute the SELECT before either INSERT commits, so both see zero matching rows and both proceed to insert. This is a textbook check-then-act race that cannot be fixed by adding retries or synchronised blocks at the application layer — the fix must be enforced at the database level with a UNIQUE constraint.

documents.body: Two concurrent refund requests load the same account entity at version 5. The first request commits its credit and bumps the version to 6. documents.body: A three-step payment saga (Debit → Reserve → Charge) fails at the Charge step and triggers a compensating un-debit event. documents.body: A payment processing service uses manual offset commits (enable.auto.commit=false) to guarantee delivery. documents.body: Account balances are cached in Redis with a 60-second TTL. At the moment of expiry, 1,000 concurrent API requests all miss the cache simultaneously, all query PostgreSQL, and all attempt to repopulate Redis — the database is overwhelmed and some requests return stale or inconsistent balances. All threads see null, all issue a database query in parallel, and all write back to Redis — a classic thundering herd. documents.subtitle: Redisson TTL shorter than processing time allows a second pod to acquire the lock — duplicate payment
documents.body: Payment deduplication relies on a Redisson distributed lock with a 5-second TTL. When a slow downstream payment gateway causes processing to take 6 seconds, the lock expires before unlock() is called. A second pod then acquires the lock and processes the same payment, issuing a duplicate transaction. Customers are charged twice for the same transaction; chargeback rates increase; card network fines are triggered when duplicate-transaction rates exceed thresholds. When lock.lock() is called with an explicit leaseTime, Redisson sets the Redis key TTL to exactly that value. If the holder's operation outlasts the TTL, Redis automatically deletes the key and any other node can acquire the lock immediately — even though the original holder is still inside the critical section. The result is two simultaneous holders of the same "exclusive" lock, breaking the mutual-exclusion guarantee.

The reconciliation consumer cannot tell that an event was already processed, so each redelivered event is inserted as a new row and added to the daily total again.

documents.title: Card Authorisation and Clearing with a Fraud Hook and Resilience
documents.body: Source code: examples/capstone 3 card authorisation · run mvn test pl capstone 3 card authorisation am from examples/ The issuer side of a card payment: authorise (hold), capture (clearing), reverse, refund, chargeback. Plus a fraud check that is allowed to be slow or down without taking authorisations down with it. Spring Boot 4.0.9, Spring Framework 7.0 resilience annotations, Resilience4j 2.4.0, PostgreSQL 17. The problem A card payment is not one event. The merchant first asks "can this card pay 100.00?" (authorisation, which places a hold). Later it asks for the money (capture, which happens at clearing), possibly in several parts. Later still there may be a refund, or the cardholder may dispute it (chargeback). Each step is only legal in certain states, and amounts must never exceed what came before. Every authorisation also calls a fraud engine. Authorisations have tight latency budgets: the cardholder is standing at a till. If the fraud engine is slow, we must not wait for it. If it is down, we must not hammer it. And we need a written rule for what to decide without a score. Risk Fix Canonical lesson Capture more than authorised, refund more than captured State machine on a sealed command type + DB CHECK constraints Card payments Two partial captures at once exceed the auth @Version optimistic locking + Spring 7 @Retryable re validates the loser Optimistic locking Merchant retries a capture operation id (Idempotency Key) is the primary key of the audit row Idempotency patterns Slow fraud engine stalls authorisations 300 ms read timeout on the HTTP Service Client Timeout engineering Fraud engine down: every call waits for the timeout Resilience4j circuit breaker Circuit breaker Fraud calls use up all capacity Bulkhead: Spring 7 @ConcurrencyLimit(policy = REJECT) Bulkhead No score: approve or decline? Explicit fallback: approve ≤ 50.00 ("stand in"), decline above Fallback patterns Architecture The fraud call happens before the database transaction, so a slow fraud engine never holds a database connection. Key decisions and trade offs Decision Why Cost / when not to Sealed CardCommand + switch pattern matching Adding a command (e.g. IncrementalAuth ) will not compile until the state machine handles it Java 21; slightly more types. Optimistic locking + @Retryable for captures Contention on one authorisation is rare; retries are cheap and re validate the rules Under heavy contention on one row, use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE instead (see capstone 2). @Retryable wraps a TransactionTemplate , not @Transactional Each retry must be a new transaction. Proxy ordering of two annotations is easy to get wrong. One explicit line of code. Spring 7 @ConcurrencyLimit (REJECT) as bulkhead Built into the framework, no extra library; rejects instead of queueing Semaphore only. No queue, no metrics of its own. Resilience4j Bulkhead has more knobs. Resilience4j circuit breaker Spring Framework 7 has retry and concurrency limits but no circuit breaker One more dependency (used programmatically, no Boot starter needed). Fail open below 50.00, closed above Small purchases keep working during an outage; the large loss tail is protected The limit is a risk decision, not an engineering one. 50.00 here is illustrative. Store a card token , never the PAN Keeps this service out of most PCI DSS cardholder data scope Requires a tokenisation service. The API rejects raw PANs at the edge. documents.title: Settlement and Reconciliation Pipeline (CAMT.053 ingest, matching, breaks)
documents.body: Source code: examples/capstone 4 reconciliation · run mvn test pl capstone 4 reconciliation am from examples/ Every evening the bank sends a statement. This service proves that what the bank booked equals what our ledger expected, explains every difference, and gives operations a controlled way to clear them. Spring Boot 4.0.9, Java 21, StAX, PostgreSQL 17. The problem Our ledger says "we sent 110.00 to supplier X". The bank statement says 100.00 left the account. Was there a fee? A partial payment? A bug? Reconciliation compares two independent records of the same money and turns every disagreement into a break : a typed, owned, audited item someone must resolve. Regulators and auditors expect breaks to be explained, not deleted. Bank files are untrusted input, may arrive twice, may be corrected and re sent, and may be large. The pipeline must be safe, idempotent and explainable. Concern Fix Canonical lesson Hostile XML (XXE, entity expansion) StAX with DTDs and external entities disabled Secure coding Truncated or corrupted file Opening + credits − debits must equal closing balance, or reject ISO 20022 Same file delivered twice SHA 256 of the bytes is UNIQUE ; re delivery returns the first result Idempotency patterns Two files for one account processed at once pg advisory xact lock(hashtext(iban)) + UNIQUE(ledger item id) on matches Pessimistic locking and advisory locks Matching rules Pure, unit tested Matcher : exact → mismatch → fuzzy → leftovers Scenario I: reconciliation mismatches Breaks "fixed" without trace Workflow OPEN → INVESTIGATING → RESOLVED, append only break event , optimistic locking, four eyes on large write offs Audit trails Architecture Matching rules, in order: Rule Outcome 1 Same EndToEndId , amount, direction MATCHED (EXACT) 2 Same EndToEndId , different amount or direction AMOUNT MISMATCH break 3 No id ( NOTPROVIDED ): one unmatched ledger item with the same amount and direction, value date within ±2 days MATCHED (FUZZY AMOUNT DATE) 3b …more than one candidate AMBIGUOUS break (a human chooses; never guess) 4 Bank line left over MISSING IN LEDGER (fees, unexpected credits, fraud) 5 Ledger item left over and older than 2 days MISSING IN BANK (newer ones are in transit , not breaks) 6 Bank reference seen before DUPLICATE IN BANK A later statement that books a missing item auto resolves the old MISSING IN BANK break, with an audit event. Key decisions and trade offs Decision Why Cost / when not to StAX streaming parser, local names only Memory stays flat; works for any camt.053.001.xx version Supports a subset: one statement per file, one TxDtls per entry (no batch bookings). Reject an unbalanced file outright A partial file silently creates false breaks Operations must chase the bank for a corrected file. Same statement id, different bytes → 409 A silent "replace" would rewrite history Corrections need a manual, audited path. Fuzzy match only when the candidate is unique A wrong auto match hides a real break; a false break only costs time More manual work for same amount payments. Timing tolerance before MISSING IN BANK Banks book a day or two later; flagging immediately creates noise A real loss is seen 2 days later. Tune per bank and rail (instant rails need minutes). Four eyes on write offs above 100.00 Standard control against one person hiding losses Slower resolution; the threshold is illustrative. One transaction per file All or nothing ingest; simple recovery Very large files hold the lock longer (see load test). documents.title: Instant P2P Transfer API with OAuth2, Per-Tenant Rate Limiting and Webhooks
documents.body: Source code: examples/capstone 5 instant p2p · run mvn test pl capstone 5 instant p2p am from examples/ A multi tenant API that moves money between users instantly, trusts nothing but a verified token, keeps one noisy tenant from hurting the others, and tells each tenant's backend about every transfer reliably. Spring Boot 4.0.9, Spring Security 7.0, Redis 7.4, PostgreSQL 17. The problem Several fintech partners (tenants) run their users' P2P payments on our platform. Four things must hold: 1. Identity comes from the token, not the request. A user can spend only from their own account, and a tenant never sees another tenant's data. 2. Fairness. One tenant's traffic spike or buggy retry loop must not starve the others. 3. Reliable notification. Each tenant's backend gets a signed webhook for every completed transfer, even if it is down for a while, without us holding resources while it is slow. 4. No SSRF. Tenants register webhook URLs; we must not let them aim our servers at internal targets. Concern Fix Canonical lesson Authentication Stateless OAuth2 resource server: signature, issuer, expiry and audience validated OAuth2 and JWT Authorisation Scopes via @PreAuthorize ; ownership checked in the SQL (OWASP API1 BOLA) OWASP Top 10 Fairness Redis token bucket per tenant, atomic Lua, server time; 429 + Retry After Distributed rate limiting Double spend Single statement conditional debit ... WHERE balance minor = :m ; fixed lock order Scenario C: double spending Lost or duplicated webhook Delivery row in the transfer transaction; lease, retry with backoff + full jitter, then DEAD Retry patterns, Transactional outbox Spoofed webhook HMAC SHA256 over id.timestamp.body ; receiver compares in constant time API security SSRF via webhook URL (OWASP API7) https only, no private/loopback/link local targets, no redirects Secure coding Architecture Webhook retry, failure then recovery: Key decisions and trade offs Decision Why Cost / when not to Tenant and user only from JWT claims Headers and bodies are attacker controlled Requires the identity provider to issue a tenant id claim. 404 (not 403) for other people's resources Does not confirm that an id exists Slightly harder debugging for honest clients. CSRF disabled Bearer tokens are not sent automatically by browsers; no cookies, no sessions Would be wrong if you later add cookie based login. Token bucket in Redis + Lua Atomic across all instances; allows bursts up to capacity Redis on the hot path; mitigated by a 200 ms timeout and fail open with an alert. Fail closed would turn a Redis outage into a full outage. Redis TIME inside the script App servers' clocks can drift Requires Redis ≥ 5 effect replication (default since Redis 5). Rate limit after authentication The bucket is per verified tenant; anonymous floods are stopped earlier (WAF / gateway) An unauthenticated flood still costs JWT validation; put a coarse per IP limit at the edge. Webhook lease instead of FOR UPDATE during the call A slow tenant endpoint never holds a DB connection or row lock A crash mid delivery waits for the lease (30 s) before a retry. Full jitter backoff, max 8 attempts, then DEAD Spreads retries; bounded effort; DEAD rows are replayable by ops Delivery is at least once: receivers must de duplicate on Webhook Id . Conditional UPDATE instead of a full ledger Smallest correct debit; this capstone focuses on the API edge Capstone 2 has the double entry ledger. In production this service posts to it. The tests act as a tiny identity provider: they generate an RSA key pair, sign tokens with it, and configure a JwtDecoder that checks signature, issuer, expiry and audience. Boot's issuer uri decoder backs off because a JwtDecoder bean exists.
